problem: Existing VLAs have billions of parameters, need costly large-scale pre-training, and are limited to fixed-base manipulation. Lightweight VLAs (TinyVLA, MiniVLA, SmolVLA) have not systematically studied practicality and cannot do mobile manipulation.
motivation: Practical deployment on consumer GPUs and mobile platforms requires small, pretraining-free models that work across embodiments and under visual domain randomization. The authors build a benchmark (CEBench) and use it to find which design choices (multi-view input, proprioception, chunking, training curriculum, action space) let a small VLA match large ones.
key_idea: A 0.5B LLaVA-OneVision-based VLA with merged multi-view image, proprioception tokens, discrete action chunking and a direction+value token hybrid action space, trained by in-domain post-training then fine-tuning without cross-embodiment pre-training, does both manipulation and navigation.
insight: Small VLAs can rival 7B models when key design choices are right. Ablations show merging views into one image (CALVIN Avg. Len. 3.68 vs 1.50 for concatenated tokens), proprioception tokenization (3.68 vs 3.09 MLP) and chunk size 5 (3.68 vs 2.25 at size 1) matter most. Post-training on in-domain multi-task data beats pre-training (Open Laptop 38% vs 20%), and direction+value tokens beat plain action-value tokens for mobile manipulation (4/10 vs 2/10, 4/10 vs 1/10).
method: Backbone: pre-trained LLaVA-OneVision-0.5B VLM, autoregressive with discrete action tokens (256 bins, chunk size 5).
Multi-view input: first- and third-person images vertically concatenated into one composite image to reduce tokens and match VLM training.
Proprioception tokenizer: proprioceptive state converted to tokens (inverse of the action de-tokenizer) instead of an MLP projector.
Two-stage training: post-training on multi-task in-domain data, then task-specific fine-tuning (fine-tuning on a single 4090; no cross-embodiment pre-training).

Hybrid action space: navigation as direction token (forward/left/right/stop) plus value token (distance/angle); manipulation value tokens appended after 'stop'; a special <Navigation> token after the instruction triggers mobile manipulation.

CEBench: CALVIN (single arm), RoboTwin (14.4k sim trajectories, 36 tasks, 400 per task), and real-world Cobot-Magic data (1.6k trajectories, 8 tasks) including mobile tasks, with domain-randomized evaluation.

setting.training_data: CALVIN official data (ABC->D, 1 epoch post-training, ~6h on 8 H100); RoboTwin 14.4k sim trajectories; 1.6k real trajectories (200 per task, 8 tasks incl. 2 mobile); 2 epochs post-training + 8 epochs fine-tuning; no cross-embodiment pre-training
setting.observation: multi-view RGB (first- and third-person, merged into one image) + proprioception; real robot RGB 480x640 at 30Hz
setting.action_space: discrete tokenized action chunks (size 5, 256 bins); navigation via direction token (forward/turn left/turn right/stop) + value token

numbers.extra: no cross-embodiment pre-training; 1 epoch post-training, no fine-tuning

numbers_note: Mobile manipulation results given only as 10-episode counts (ablation table: 4/10 fetch bottles, 4/10 open drawer with direction+value tokens) and a figure; ACT baseline 10%. No navigation benchmarks (R2R, ObjectNav, etc.) are reported.
results: On CALVIN ABC->D the 0.5B model gets Avg. Len. 3.68, beating OpenVLA 7B (3.27) and RoboFlamingo 3B (2.47), and is on par with its own 7B variant (3.75). On RoboTwin it gets 40.3% Seen / 28.6% DR, versus RDT (large) 48.9% / 11.4%, and it beats ACT and DP. In the real world it gets 44.2% Seen / 30.7% DR versus ACT 18.6% / 3.0% and TinyVLA 17.5% / 4.2%.
limitations: Mobile manipulation evaluated on only 2 tasks with 10 trials each, with modest success (4/10); the navigation is coarse and only compared with ACT
Still trails the large RDT on Seen RoboTwin (40.3 vs 48.9) and lacks a pre-training comparison at scale; findings are based on limited ablations on CALVIN/RoboTwin
